name: Hydroxypinacolone retinoate

lead: Hydroxypinacolone retinoate (HPR) is an ester of retinoic acid used in over-the-counter skincare. Its best-known commercial form is Granactive Retinoid, a trademarked 10% HPR solution from Grant Industries [1]. It is marketed as a retinoid for lines and acne with less irritation than retinol or tretinoin.

Research is modest. Small Italian studies tested HPR-containing gels in acne, Chinese studies tested it in anti-aging serums, and laboratory work compares it with other retinoids. Most human studies use combination formulas, so conclusions about HPR alone are limited.

paras: Manufacturer-derived descriptions say HPR can bind retinoid receptors directly without needing conversion, which is claimed to explain lower irritation [1]. Independent clinical comparisons with tretinoin are not reported in the studies reviewed.

Trials of HPR-containing products report mild local effects such as dryness, peeling, erythema and burning in about 15% of participants in one open study [2]. A laboratory study found retinoid products often lose potency with storage and light [4]. Retinoic acid itself is banned in cosmetics because of safety concerns [11]. Pregnancy safety data for HPR were not found in the sources reviewed.

lead: Hydroxypinacolone retinoate (HPR) is a synthetic retinoid ester that appears in cosmetic skincare, either on its own or alongside retinol or retinyl propionate [1][2][3]. A 2021 stability study treated it as a newer retinoid in commercial cosmetics alongside retinol, retinyl palmitate and beta-carotene [4]. It is sold under the trade name Granactive Retinoid, a trademarked mixture of 10% HPR in dimethyl isosorbide developed by Grant Industries, according to Grokipedia, which dates the product's introduction to late 2014 and says it was licensed to brands including The Ordinary [5].

Sources describe its chemistry slightly differently: a 2015 clinical paper calls it a synthetic ester of 9-cis-retinoic acid, whereas Grokipedia describes it as the pinacolyl ester of all-trans retinoic acid [1][5]. Marketing materials describe it as binding retinoid receptors directly and as less irritating than retinol [5].
Evidence on HPR in people consists of small open or comparative studies, most using combination products for acne or photoaging, plus in-vitro and zebrafish work [1][6][7][2][8][9].
infobox: HPR; Granactive Retinoid (trademarked 10% HPR in dimethyl isosorbide) [5]
Cosmetic ingredient; retinoic acid itself is banned in cosmetics [12]

paras: HPR is incorporated into serums and creams aimed at wrinkles and photoaging, and into gels for mild to moderate acne [1][2][9].

Acne. In a sponsor-free, open, multicenter pilot study, 98 patients aged 15 to 40 with mild to moderate facial acne used a gel combining 0.1% HPR, 1% retinol in glycospheres and 2% papain once daily for 12 weeks; the authors reported a 41% mean reduction in Global Acne Grading System score and a 40.8% reduction in total lesions, with mild to moderate local effects (dryness, peeling, erythema, burning) in 15.3% and no discontinuations [1]. In a 12-month maintenance study, 40 patients with moderate acne who had achieved remission on oral isotretinoin then used an HPR and retinol glycosphere gel; 6 of 39 completers (15.38%) relapsed and no adverse events were reported [6]. Other small Italian studies tested HPR in mixtures with azelaic acid and alpha-hydroxy acids plus a probiotic (30 patients, 60 days) and with an antimicrobial peptide, salicylic acid, glycolic acid and niacinamide (2-month prospective study) [9][10]. All are uncontrolled or combination studies, so HPR's separate contribution is not isolated.

Skin aging. A 2023 paper combined in-vitro fibroblast work with an in-vivo serum evaluation to test an HPR and retinyl propionate combination for dermal remodeling and irritation, and a 2025 comparative study examined a topical HPR-peptide product against a single fractional CO2 laser treatment over 16 weeks in women with moderate photodamage [2][8]. A comparison of five retinoids, including HPR, evaluated anti-inflammatory and anti-oxidative activity in vitro and in vivo for photoaging [7]. A nanoparticle formulation of retinyl propionate and HPR was reported to have high stability and low irritation in a 2023 paper [3].
Laboratory safety work. A zebrafish study of a microencapsulated HPR ingredient assessed irritation and developmental toxicity compared with a reference HPR product [11].
Head-to-head human trials comparing HPR with tretinoin or retinol as single agents were not found in the studies reviewed.

In the acne pilot, 15.3% of patients had mild to moderate dryness, peeling, erythema or burning [1]. Skin intolerance with retinoids in general is cited as the motivation for HPR combinations in anti-aging work, particularly among Chinese users [2]. The zebrafish study reported that an HPR reference product increased an irritation measure at a lower concentration than the microencapsulated ingredient, and calculated teratogenicity indices for both [11].

A 2021 study of 12 commercial cosmetics reported that retinoids degraded over 6 months in almost all products, with declines of 0 to 80% at 25 degrees C and 40 to 100% at 40 degrees C, with light causing more degradation than heat; HPR was among the compounds tested [4]. A separate quality-control study examined labeling and retinoid content in commercial products and screened for retinoic acid, which is prohibited in cosmetics [12].

According to Grokipedia, Grant Industries introduced Granactive Retinoid in December 2014, registered the trademark in 2017, and licensed it to consumer brands including The Ordinary, which began featuring it around 2016 [5]. The sources reviewed contain no looksmaxxing forum discussion specific to HPR.
